column4: F: Why is construction moving from flat drawings to a digital twin?
column5: F: Why is construction moving from flat drawings to a digital twin?

column3: §FILM_FACT details_sheet · a flat sheet, then the shed as a model
column4: M: A flat sheet. And the same shed, as a model.
column5: M: Hold that question. Here is a flat sheet, the shed's {details_sheet}. And here is the same shed, as a model. Nothing answered yet.

column4: M: Before the screen: a mark made so it can be read again.
column5: M: Before the screen. Every drawing, every account, began as a mark made so it can be read again.

column4: M: Nine thousand years ago, someone engraved a plan on stone, to scale.
column5: M: Nine thousand years ago, someone engraved a plan on stone, to scale.

column4: M: In Uruk, a scribe pressed accounts into clay.
column5: M: Five thousand years ago, a scribe in Uruk pressed accounts into clay.

column4: M: In Djoser's time, an architect sketched a curve, with its heights in cubits.
column5: M: In Djoser's time, an architect sketched a curve, with its heights in cubits. | F: Why write it down at all? | M: So the next person could read it again.

column4: M: Lines went digital in 1982. An open model came in the nineties.
column5: M: Then lines went digital: AutoCAD and DXF, in 1982. And in the nineties, IFC: an open model every tool can reuse.

column4: M: Sixty years, one direction.
column5: M: Sixty years, one direction. Each step lets the information be reused by more people, and more tools.

column3: chart 0c row: lines on a screen
column4: M: First, lines on a screen. Read by a person.
column5: M: First, lines on a screen. Reused by a person, reading it.

column4: M: Then objects that carry data.
column5: M: Then objects that carry data. Reused by the same tool.

column4: M: Then one open model that every tool can read: IFC.
column5: M: Then, in the nineties, one open shared model that every tool can read: IFC. Reused by any tool.

column4: M: Standards and mandates followed.
column5: M: Standards and mandates followed, so the information is managed for the whole life of a building.

column4: M: And a live digital twin.
column5: M: And at the top, a live digital twin: the concept dates from 2002.

column4: M: This work starts at the bottom: a raw drawing set, an open model, reused.
column5: M: Each step moved the information one stage further from the person who made it. This work starts at the bottom: a raw 2D drawing set, an open IFC model, reused downstream.

column4: F: So it's a history of drawing? | M: No.
column5: F: So it's a history of drawing? | M: No. Look at the marks.

column4: M: Every mark is hollow: recorded for a person to read.
column5: M: For four and a half thousand years, every mark is hollow. Recorded for a person to read.

column4: M: Even CAD, in 1982: lines a person measures.
column5: M: Even CAD, in 1982: lines a person measures, notes as text.

column4: F: And the stars? | M: A tool reads those too.
column5: F: And the stars? | M: That is where a tool reads it too. The shed's own note on its concrete mix prices the concrete and sets the stiffness of the frame.

column4: M: An open model can carry all of it.
column5: M: And an open IFC model can carry all of it, down every row. Nobody typed it twice.

column4: M: Not for the picture. For the information: entered once, reused forever.
column5: M: That is why construction goes digital. Not for the picture. For the information: entered once, reused forever.

column3: §FILM_FACT dims_drawn / dim_a_say / dim_b_say · the DETAILS sheet, a beam section enlarged
column4: M: One drawing, entered once: {dims_drawn} dimensions drawn.
column5: M: Here is where it starts: one drawing, entered once by a drafter. The details sheet, with {dims_drawn} dimensions drawn, and the bar labels with their diameter sign. This beam spans {dim_a_say} and {dim_b_say}.

column4: M: And a note: mix {ratio_say}. Written once.
column5: M: And a note: footings, columns and grade beams are cast at {ratio_say}. Written once, by a person, for a person. | F: Is that all? | M: So far.

column4: M: The sheet is marked NOTES: {notes_read} general notes read.
column5: M: The sheet is marked as notes, not as an error. The model read {notes_read} general notes from it.

column3: §FILM_FACT n_ratio_footing / n_ratio_column / ratio_say · a footing selected
column4: M: A footing. {n_ratio_footing} footings and {n_ratio_column} columns carry the mix.
column5: M: Now a footing, selected. The note was read, not retyped, by a tool this time: {n_ratio_footing} footings and {n_ratio_column} columns carry the mix {ratio_say}. | F: Where do I see it? | M: The Modeller has no properties panel yet. So here is the footing's own export.

column3: §FILM_FACT foot_sched_t / foot_drawn_m · the footing's property lines in the IFC, enlarged
column4: M: Its properties, in the model's own IFC: the note, its sheet, the schedule.
column5: M: These are the footing's properties, in the model's own IFC file: the casting ratio, the sheet and handle it came from, and the schedule's thickness, {foot_sched_t}. The footing is drawn {foot_drawn_m} metres thick: the same.

column3: §FILM_FACT imp_k1_say / imp_k2_say / imp_k3_say · Measure impact, ranked rows enlarged
column4: M: Which defaults matter to the bill? {imp_k1_say} first.
column5: M: Reused for cost. First, which defaults matter. Measure impact ranks them by what each one moves in the bill: {imp_k1_say} first, then {imp_k2_say}, then {imp_k3_say}.

column3: §FILM_FACT sor_a_say / sor_page_a / sor_book / bill_total · the SoR row enlarged
column4: M: The note chose the price row: item {sor_a_say}.
column5: M: And the bill. Footings and columns are priced at item {sor_a_say}, page {sor_page_a} of the {sor_book}. The drawing's own note picked the row: read again, by a tool this time. | F: And the total? | M: {bill_total}.

column3: §FILM_FACT mr_marks / gb_mark / gb_tags · the advisory enlarged
column4: M: Checked across the set: {gb_mark} is tagged and detailed, but not modelled.
column5: M: Reused for checks. The model compares your tags, your details and the bodies, across {mr_marks} marks. The mark {gb_mark} is tagged {gb_tags} times and has a detail, but no body is modelled. | F: Is that an error? | M: No. An advisory.

column3: the GB-1 tag on the foundation sheet, enlarged
column4: M: Here is its tag on the foundation sheet.
column5: M: Here is the tag, on the foundation layout. The checks found it, and found nothing modelled under it.

column3: §FILM_FACT ls_total_kN / ls_parts · the Load Summary own-weight card enlarged
column4: M: A ballpark weight: {ls_total_kN} kilonewtons of own weight.
column5: M: And a ballpark for the engineer: the model's own weight, {ls_total_kN} kilonewtons, across {ls_parts} parts. A starting point, pending the engineer's analysis. Not a design.

column3: §FILM_FACT ifc_schema · the IFC file as text, header enlarged
column4: M: Now the handover: an IFC file.
column5: M: Now the handover. The model is written as an IFC file, the open standard, so any BIM tool can open it. It is a plain text file. It begins like this.

column3: §FILM_FACT fc_note · the strength property in the file, enlarged
column4: M: The concrete strength note travels inside it.
column5: M: And here, inside the file, the concrete's strength travels as a property, from the sheet's own note: {fc_note}. Nothing lost on the way.

column4: M: Reused for structure: an analytical model, from the IFC.
column5: M: Reused for structure. Export, analytical model: the same frame as joints, members and supports, for STAAD. The strength note became the concrete's stiffness.

column3: §FILM_FACT st_joints / st_members / st_supports · the .std sections enlarged
column4: M: {st_joints} joints, {st_members} members, {st_supports} supports.
column5: M: {st_joints} joints, in metres. {st_members} members, each from joint to joint. And {st_supports} supports, every column base on a footing.

column3: §FILM_FACT parity_set_vs_ifc · a fresh Modeller, only the IFC, the two files compared
column4: M: Through the open standard: {parity_set_vs_ifc}, byte for byte.
column5: M: The proof. A fresh Modeller, no drawings, only the IFC file. Its model file is {parity_set_vs_ifc}, byte for byte, to the one made from the drawings. The same model, through the open standard. Nothing lost on the way.

column3: §FILM_FACT m7_file · another IFC through the same Export
column4: M: Any model, not just this one. Another IFC.
column5: M: Any model, not just this one. Here is another IFC, a structural model with nothing to do with this shed. Same Export, same builder.

column3: §FILM_FACT m7_members / m7_joints / m7_supports / m7_elements / m7_with_evidence / m7_fc_missing · the status line enlarged
column4: M: {m7_members} members, {m7_joints} joints, {m7_supports} supports. What it lacks is listed.
column5: M: {m7_members} members, {m7_joints} joints, {m7_supports} supports, from {m7_elements} elements. This model states no concrete strength, so {m7_fc_missing} findings say so, and no stiffness is given: the engineer states it. What it lacks is listed, never guessed.

column4: M: The engineer's judgement is not reused. It is still theirs.
column5: M: What it does not do: the engineer's analysis and design, live, wind and seismic loads, or bars from the details. The engineer's judgement is not reused. It is still theirs.

column4: M: Entered once. Reused at every step. Never retyped.
column5: M: One note on a drawing. A property, a price, a check, an open file, the stiffness of a frame. Entered once. Reused at every step. Never retyped.

column4: F: So why? | M: A drawing is read once. A twin is reused forever.
column5: F: So why the move from flat drawings to a digital twin? | M: A drawing is read once. A twin is reused forever.
